context: light factory · panel processing lines, finishing line and dust extraction

brief.intro: New to this project type? A modern furniture factory is mostly a panel-processing line. Boards (chipboard, MDF) are cut to size on beam saws, their edges are covered on edge-banding machines, holes and grooves are made on CNC drilling and routing machines, and the parts are sorted, assembled or flat-packed. Solid-wood parts go through moulders and sanders. A finishing line sprays and dries lacquer or paint. Upholstered furniture adds cutting, sewing and foam departments. The building is a plain hall. What needs care is the dust-extraction system — ducts from every machine to large filters outside, with spark detection because wood dust burns and explodes — the spray-finishing area with its ventilation and fire protection, and compressed air everywhere.

glossary.plain: a saw that cuts stacks of boards to size.
gluing a strip onto the cut edge of a panel.
a computer-controlled machine that drills, routes and grooves parts.
cutting many different parts from one board in an optimised pattern.
the line that sands, coats and dries the surface.
the duct and filter system that removes chips and dust from every machine.
sensors that spot a spark in a duct and quench it before it reaches the filter.
producing each order individually, controlled by software, instead of large runs.

must_get_right: Design dust extraction with the machine layout — duct routes, filter position and capacity are fixed by the machines and are expensive to change.
Spark detection, explosion venting and sprinklers must be complete and tested before production; wood dust is a real explosion hazard.
The finishing area needs its own ventilation, fire protection and environmental permit (solvent emissions).
Linked lines depend on software and conveyors; allow integration time after the individual machines are accepted.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar for construction; equipment installation may run extended shifts under vendor supervision. Commissioning follows the vendor's programme, and hot commissioning runs continuously once started.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Layout freeze → floor and building → machinery installation in process order → dust extraction, air and power → safety-system tests → machine acceptance → line integration → first products. The critical path runs through the machinery delivery and the dust-extraction system.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: late machinery, extraction undersized or unbalanced, finishing-line permit, and software integration of linked lines. Contingency is held before first deliveries.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
